solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Emergency road layer ought to put in more granite

parts.note: granite is hard, so more granite is HARDER
ought to = should

explanation.surface: A road builder is told to lay down more granite.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures the workman who lays the road; the definition is instead a layer of the road itself, the strip kept for emergencies.
explanation.definitionFit: The hard shoulder is the paved strip beside a motorway where a car may stop in an emergency.

clue.text: The short brush enters up most piping

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the whole construction is read from bottom to top, so it is reversed
enters says one piece goes inside the other, the brush piece within the trimmed word
short means the word loses its last letter, so the is trimmed by one

parts.note: taken as written before it is cut short
a brush is a brief fight or scuffle, which is also a set-to

explanation.surface: A cryptic picture of a brush pushed up a pipe to clean it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brush' here is a scuffle, a set-to, not a cleaning tool, and 'piping' is the 'piping hot' sense, not plumbing.
explanation.definitionFit: Piping hot means extremely hot, so the most piping thing is the hottest one.

clue.text: Order to dispel mob's former capital judgment

parts.note: Rio de Janeiro was Brazil's capital until 1960
tact = good judgment in dealing with people

explanation.surface: A crowd's former capital punishment, as if a mob once passed death sentences.
explanation.walkthrough: Capital judgment reads as a death sentence, but the phrase splits: capital goes with former, and judgment stands alone.
explanation.definitionFit: The Riot Act was the British law read aloud to order an unruly crowd to disperse.

clue.text: Odd selection of sayings encapsulating these collected works?

definitions.note: syntheses are things put together, so collected works in a loose sense; the plural matches

indicators.note: encapsulating means enclosing as in a capsule, so the odd letters wrap around the word these
an odd selection takes the letters in odd-numbered places, first, third, fifth and seventh, of sayings

parts.note: the word whose odd letters are taken

explanation.surface: An anthology of quotations that includes these very writings among its collected works.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark warns that 'collected works' is not the literary sense but things assembled from parts.
explanation.definitionFit: A synthesis is a whole formed by combining separate elements, so syntheses are combinations or things collected together.

clue.text: Old hit for Rolling Stones

indicators.note: Rolling suggests turning over, so the word for hit is read backwards

parts.note: to slap is to hit with an open hand

explanation.surface: An old chart hit by the Rolling Stones, the rock band.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rolling Stones' reads as the band's name, but 'Rolling' reverses SLAP and 'Stones' is the definition, meaning gems.
explanation.definitionFit: Opals are precious gemstones, and in jewellery any gem is commonly called a stone.

clue.text: Scaly river beast rearing up

indicators.note: in a down clue, rearing up turns the letters upside down

parts.note: r = river
a beast is an animal

explanation.surface: A scaly creature, perhaps a crocodile, rises up out of a river.
explanation.walkthrough: Scaly reads as the beast's skin, but it is the definition: made of thin flakes or layers.
explanation.definitionFit: Laminar means arranged in thin layers or plates, like scales.

clue.text: Half-worn flea collar retaining medium protection on one side

parts.note: the second half of FLEA
a ruff is a frilled collar
m = medium, as on clothing labels

explanation.surface: A pet's flea collar, half worn out, still has some protective medicine in it.
explanation.walkthrough: The flea collar invites a pet scene; the definition is cryptic, since each earmuff guards one side of the head.
explanation.definitionFit: An earmuff is a pad that protects one ear from cold, one side of the head.

clue.text: Bucks and more in company releases

parts.note: at home = in
co = company
releases = unties

explanation.surface: A firm releasing dollars and more, as in a company paying out bucks.
explanation.walkthrough: Bucks looks like dollars; it is Buckinghamshire, one of the Home Counties, the counties surrounding London.
explanation.definitionFit: Buckinghamshire (Bucks) is one of the Home Counties that ring London, so Bucks and more are the Home Counties.

clue.text: Couple bunging old vase no longer of use

parts.note: o = old
an urn is a vase
a couple is two

explanation.surface: Two people throw out an old vase they no longer use.
explanation.walkthrough: Bunging reads as throwing away; in the wordplay it means stuffing something in, as you bung things into a bag.
explanation.definitionFit: Something outworn is worn out and no longer serviceable.

clue.text: Approved of plug diameter on sink in Slough

parts.note: to plug a product is to advertise it; an ad
to mire is to sink in a slough, a bog
d = diameter

explanation.surface: Someone praises a sink plug of the right width, fitted in Slough.
explanation.walkthrough: Slough is capitalised to look like the English town west of London; here it is a swamp, and to mire is to sink in one.
explanation.definitionFit: To admire is to regard with approval.

clue.text: Licensed bar limits salted nuts and charcuterie

indicators.note: nuts = crazy, so the letters are scrambled

parts.note: LICENSED without its first and last letters
anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A pub serving salted nuts and cold meats as bar snacks.
explanation.walkthrough: Salted nuts look like a bar snack; nuts is the anagram signal and salted is fodder. Limits are the outer letters of the word before bar.
explanation.definitionFit: Charcuterie is both cured meats and the shop that sells them, a delicatessen.

clue.text: Two types of wood on European bunk

parts.note: e = European
YEW and ASH, two trees

explanation.surface: A European bunk bed made of two different woods.
explanation.walkthrough: Bunk looks like a bed; it is the definition in the sense of nonsense.
explanation.definitionFit: Bunk and eyewash both mean nonsense or humbug.

clue.text: Animal barking unless holding its lead

definitions.note: used as an adjective meaning physical or carnal

indicators.note: barking is British slang for mad, so the letters go wild and are rearranged
holding means the word unless keeps a letter within it

parts.note: its refers back to Animal, and its lead is that word's first letter

explanation.surface: A dog barks at everything unless it is held on its lead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Animal' looks like the barking dog but is an adjective for the definition. 'its lead' is A, the first letter of Animal; 'holding' puts it inside UNLESS to give UANLESS, and 'barking' (British slang for mad) rearranges that.
explanation.definitionFit: Animal, as an adjective, means of the body and its physical appetites, as sensual does.

clue.text: Music group centre to concoct etudes

indicators.note: the answer sits in the middle of the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the join of the two words, from the tail of the first into the head of the second

explanation.surface: A band's central figure composes studies for them to play.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer straddles concoct and etudes. Etudes are musical studies, which keeps the whole scene musical.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: octet names any ensemble of eight players, as quartet names four.

clue.text: Sleepy from poor sci-fi novel

indicators.note: novel = new, so the letters are rearranged into a new form

parts.note: anagram fodder, 9 letters

explanation.surface: A reader nodding off over a badly written science-fiction book.
explanation.walkthrough: Novel sits naturally after sci-fi as the book, but it signals the rearrangement. Sleepy here means sleep-inducing, as a dull book is.
explanation.definitionFit: Soporific means inducing sleep, or drowsy.

clue.text: Fruit in individual one millimetre slices

parts.note: an individual is a person
I = one, the Roman numeral
mm = millimetre

explanation.surface: Someone cuts fruit into slices one millimetre thick.
explanation.walkthrough: Slices looks like the noun, thin pieces of fruit; it is a verb, with I MM cutting into PERSON.
explanation.definitionFit: The persimmon is an orange fruit, also called sharon fruit.

clue.text: Mister Joseph's eldest brother holding most of deposit back

indicators.note: SILT loses its last letter
the whole assembly is read backwards

parts.note: in Genesis, Reuben is Jacob's firstborn, Joseph's eldest brother
SILT, a river deposit, without its last letter

explanation.surface: A Mr Joseph whose eldest brother keeps back most of a deposit, like a family squabble over money.
explanation.walkthrough: Mister looks like a form of address; it is one who mists, a device that turns liquid into a fine spray.
explanation.definitionFit: A nebuliser turns liquid medicine into a mist to be breathed in, so it is literally a mister.

clue.text: Doctor's prime spot by blankets?

parts.note: by = beside

indicators.note: the prime letter of Doctor is its first

parts.note: first letter of Doctor

explanation.surface: Where a good doctor stands: right by the patient's bed.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition, with the question mark flagging that spot by blankets is a playful way of saying beside the bed.
explanation.definitionFit: A doctor's best place is the bedside, where bedside manner counts.

clue.text: Professor's one needing coat

indicators.note: a professor professes, declaring out loud, so what follows is heard rather than read

parts.note: one who lacks something is a lacker

explanation.surface: An academic who needs a coat for the cold.
explanation.walkthrough: Professor looks like an academic; here it is one who professes, declaring things out loud. Coat is the verb or noun for a layer of varnish.
explanation.definitionFit: Lacquer is a hard glossy coating.

clue.text: Praise movie withdrawing permissive parts

indicators.note: parts means separates, so this piece splits the film title in two

parts.note: E.T. is the Spielberg film about an extra-terrestrial

indicators.note: withdrawing is read as drawing back, so the word for permissive runs backwards

parts.note: lax means loose or permissive in standards

explanation.surface: Applauding a film for cutting out its racy scenes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'withdrawing permissive parts' reads as censorship, but LAX (permissive) is reversed by 'withdrawing' to XAL, which 'parts' the movie ET.
explanation.definitionFit: To exalt is to glorify or extol someone, raising them high in praise.

clue.text: Istanbul address set up ID and iron locks in flat

indicators.note: locks in means encloses, so the reversed letters surround the word for flat
in a down clue set up means placed upwards, so these letters read from the bottom
and simply joins the two pieces that are then reversed together, ID followed by iron

parts.note: Fe is the chemical symbol for iron
a fen is flat low-lying marshland, as in the Fens of eastern England

explanation.surface: A visitor's ID card and an iron are locked inside a flat in Istanbul.
explanation.walkthrough: 'set up' reverses ID and FE to EFDI, and 'locks in' puts FEN (the Fens are the flat marshland of eastern England) into it.
explanation.definitionFit: Effendi was a Turkish title of respect, a polite form of address for an educated man, akin to sir.

clue.text: Leading writer owns record collection

parts.note: arch = chief, leading, as in archbishop
the writer says I have, I've

explanation.surface: A top author owns a collection of vinyl records.
explanation.walkthrough: Record collection suggests music; it is a collection of documents. The writer of a clue refers to themselves as I.
explanation.definitionFit: An archive is a store of documents, so record collection fits in the paperwork sense, not the vinyl one.

clue.text: Batting failure masking century England's opener got

definitions.note: got in the sense of persuaded, as in got someone to do something

parts.note: in cricket the side batting is said to be in

indicators.note: masking means covering up, so the failure word hides the letters inside it

parts.note: a dud is something that fails or does not work
C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, a century

indicators.note: opener means the first letter, here of England's

parts.note: the word whose first letter, E, is used

explanation.surface: A cricket report: England's opening batsman failed while batting, missing his century.
explanation.walkthrough: The cricket surface makes 'got' sound like being dismissed, but it means persuaded, as in got him to stay.
explanation.definitionFit: To induce someone is to persuade or cause them to act, the same as getting them to do it.

clue.text: American's parking in departure area way below

indicators.note: in here means coming in instead, so one letter takes the place of another

parts.note: departure is a euphemism for death
P marks parking, the American word for what Britons call a car park

explanation.surface: Parking at the departures area of an American airport is a long way down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'departure area' reads as one place in an airport, but DEATH (departure) has its A (area) replaced by P (parking).
explanation.definitionFit: Depth is distance downwards from a surface, so something at depth lies a long way below.

clue.text: Does corrupt criminal court void fines?

indicators.note: criminal = wrong, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: COURT without its inner letters
anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A question about whether a crooked court cancels the penalties it imposes.
explanation.walkthrough: Does corrupt is an emphatic verb, standing for corrupts; the question mark ends a surface that is really a statement.
explanation.definitionFit: Infection spreads rot as corruption does; does corrupt is just the emphatic form of corrupts.

clue.text: Plane quiet with just 50 per cent aboard winter flight

indicators.note: only half of JUST is used

parts.note: to plane over water is to skim
half of JUST
p = piano, quiet

explanation.surface: A quiet plane only half full of passengers on a winter flight.
explanation.walkthrough: Plane looks like an aircraft, but it is the verb to skim; the flight is the skier's leap off the ramp.
explanation.definitionFit: A ski jump is a leap through the air on skis, a flight in winter sport.

clue.text: Large poles separating cereal crop

indicators.note: N and S go between MA and IZE, separating it

parts.note: maize is a cereal crop
N and S, the north and south poles

explanation.surface: Big posts dividing up a field of cereal.
explanation.walkthrough: Poles looks like fence posts; it is N and S, the two poles of the earth.
explanation.definitionFit: Man-size means large, big enough for a man.

clue.text: Charge seen in mobile web app

indicators.note: mobile = moving, so the letters shift about

parts.note: anagram fodder, 12 letters

explanation.surface: A fee turns up in a phone's web app.
explanation.walkthrough: Mobile sits naturally beside web app as a phone; it is the anagram signal, and seen in is fodder, not a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A search engine is a web application for finding pages.
